hlni.insight: A task label alone does not define the assessment; grading criteria determine the actual learning focus.
hlni.audienceGap: Students assume degree titles imply a universal learning experience.
hlni.viewerChange: Learns to ask for specific grading criteria to distinguish between academic paths.
hlni.support: The method separates task definition from evaluation criteria, allowing for objective comparison.
hlni.payoff: The viewer gains a concrete, repeatable method to probe course content without relying on stereotypes.

candidate.reelTitle: B.Com vs BBA: The Assessment Audit
candidate.objective: Teach students to audit assessment criteria for informed academic decisions.
candidate.targetAudience: +2 students seeking academic depth and well-supported course and career decisions

shots.name: Hook and Setup
shots.visual: A student looks at two identical project prompts on a tablet.
shots.dialogue: Choosing between B.Com and BBA? Don't just read the titles. Look at the tasks.

shots.name: The Pattern Interrupt
shots.visual: Split screen showing two different grading rubrics for the same task.
shots.dialogue: Criteria: Graded on (A) Creativity or (B) ROI calculation? The 'how' changes the focus entirely.

shots.name: Value and Payoff
shots.visual: Student holds a pen, circling an empty space on a worksheet.
shots.dialogue: To decide, ask: What are the specific grading criteria for this assignment? That question reveals the true academic path.
shots.onscreenText: What are the specific grading criteria for this assignment?
shots.cameraPerformance: Macro shot of writing on paper.

productionNotes.editing: Rhythmic cuts synchronized with text appearance.

creativeSummary.keyCreativeIdea: Shifting the comparison from degree titles to the actual assessment criteria used in coursework.

selected.title: The Assessment Audit
selected.audienceGap: Students assume a subject title (e.g., 'Business Law') implies a fixed, universal learning experience for both degrees.
selected.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
selected.viewerChange: Learns to look past labels to identify how a task is actually graded.
selected.concept: A student compares two identical-sounding project prompts and learns to audit the assessment criteria.
selected.device: Split-screen comparison of two project prompts showing how different grading criteria change the focus of the task.
selected.support: The method separates three different pieces of information; it does not assume particular course content.
methodSteps: Ask what criterion is used to assess it.
Ask what feedback is available; mark unknown answers as questions.
selected.interpretationRule: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question about the actual course or task before deciding.
selected.visibleProof: A three-column question sheet turns one vague preference into a concrete unanswered question.
selected.payoff: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question about the actual course or task before deciding.
selected.limitations: This is a question-forming aid, not a degree ranking, aptitude test or prediction of success.

demonstration.input: Two project prompts for a common business topic with different assessment rubrics.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Create a marketing strategy. Criteria: Graded on (A) Creativity or (B) ROI calculation?
demonstration.observation: Viewer identifies that the 'How' (criteria) is missing from the task prompt.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What are the specific grading criteria for this assignment?

comparedWith.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
comparedWith.device: Split-screen comparison of two project prompts showing how different grading criteria change the focus of the task.

comparedWith.hlni: A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.
comparedWith.device: A handwritten log where a student tracks a moment of confusion and turns it into a targeted question.

comparedWith.hlni: One unlabeled example does not prove which category or programme contains it. An exclusive claim needs information that actually links the example to that category.
comparedWith.device: A riddle-style presentation showing one element and asking the viewer to 'guess' the degree, followed by the reveal that it's impossible.

conceptSelection.contrast: Trust uses a structural audit of criteria to build verification habits; Connection uses a personal journal to manage anxiety via specific questioning; Discovery uses a logical reveal to expose the fallacy of jumping to conclusions based on partial data.
